name: Carla Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a family lawyer at a firm in a market town, so divorces, splitting money and homes, and arrangements for children after a break-up. I use AI every day to summarise bank statements and draft letters to the other side, which saves me hours. Then there's the other half of the job: clients crying in my office, phone calls at seven at night, sitting next to someone in court. I keep a box of tissues on my desk and get through one a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like helping someone get through the worst year of their life with their kids still okay. What wears me out is the emotion, all day, and the money. I'm paid less than at the bigger firms, and my partner's freelance, so our income goes up and down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still worth using for the dull parts, and people who dropped them were silly. In family law, the work is people, not paper, so I was never worried about being replaced. I'd post something like that and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a mild relief, but my money problems stay. I'm paid less than lawyers at the bigger firms, my partner's design work comes and goes, and we've got less than a month saved. A plateau just means the same tight months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI every day to summarise bank statements in divorce cases, which saves me a couple of hours a file. I'd start the mediation course I've been eyeing, paying it off monthly. And I'd keep a spreadsheet of every penny for a few months to find what we can cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Not thrilled, not scared. Tired, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes your partner's work come and go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's a freelance graphic designer, so it's feast or famine. Last spring he had nothing for two months, and we lived on my salary and a loan from his brother. I still feel that month in my shoulders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family law is people, not paper. How much of your day is paper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than I'd like to admit, probably half. Forms, financial disclosure, letters to the other side. The tears and the phone calls are the other half, and those are what I'm actually good at.

I'd say family law is **people, not paper**.
think: A plateau is a **mild relief**, but our money stays tight.
My partner's **freelance income** swings, and we have under a month saved.
do: Keep using AI daily on **bank statements** in divorce files.
Track **every penny** for a few months to find cuts.
S0.quote: In family law, the work is people, not paper, so I was never worried about being replaced.
fieldNote: She later admits **half her day** is paper, contradicting her public line.
A two-month **income gap** last spring still weighs on her.
She's already **planning mediation** even in the calm picture.

steps.text: Keep using AI to summarise bank statements in divorce files
Start a mediation course, paid monthly
Track every household expense in a spreadsheet for three months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say lawyers who learn the tools will be fine and those who don't will struggle. I'd also say AI can't sit with a mother who's about to lose half her time with her kids. I'd post about the good uses, like faster financial disclosure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm worried about two incomes, not one. My firm would need fewer junior lawyers for paperwork, and I'm average, so I'm not safe just because I use the tools. And my partner's design work is exactly what AI does now, so his side could dry up first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the mediation accreditation within the year, because sitting two people down to agree is hard to automate. I'd offer to train the rest of the team on our AI tools, so I'm the one they can't lose. And I'd save whatever we could, even a hundred a month, to build up one month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a bit of fight in it. I'd be busy, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner if his work dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to come and learn about mediation with me, or look at something hands-on. He'd say he's not a people person. We'd have that argument a few times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is offering to train the team a way to protect yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Completely, yes. I'd rather be useful than lucky. If the partners are choosing who stays, I want my name next to the thing that saves them money.

I'd add that AI can't sit with a parent about to **lose time** with their kids.

Offer to **train the team** on our AI tools.
Save **a hundred a month** to build one month's cushion.
feel: **Anxious**, with **fight** in it; being busy helps.

steps.text: Finish the mediation accreditation within a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need support for people now, because two years is nothing. I'd ask for rules that a human signs off on anything to do with children. I'd say the second part loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, two years ends my job as it is. The paperwork goes in 2028, and family law is mostly thinking work, so the robot date doesn't matter for me. What might last is mediation, sitting in a room with two angry people, but only if people still want a human there and can pay for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rush the mediation accreditation in the first six months and start offering sessions on Saturdays. I'd use every AI tool going to take on more clients cheaply while the work is still there. My partner and I would cut everything that isn't rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Scared for us both, and oddly determined.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would people pay a human mediator if AI can do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would. When your marriage is ending, you want someone to look you in the eye. But the ones with less money would go to the free AI, and those are most of my clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would tell me to come home and rest, which is her answer to everything. I'd tell my mum we're fine and then call my brother to ask if he knew anyone hiring. I'm the one who's meant to be sorted.

say: I'd say we need **support now**, because two years is nothing.
I'd insist a **human signs off** on anything about children.
think: The paperwork goes in **2028**, and the robot date doesn't help me.
**Mediation** might last, if people still want and can pay for a human.
do: Rush **mediation** accreditation and offer Saturday sessions.
Use **every AI tool** to take on more clients cheaply.
feel: **Alarmed** and scared for us both, yet **determined**.
S2.quote: When your marriage is ending, you want someone to look you in the eye.
fieldNote: She expects her job to **end as it is** and both incomes to be hit.
She'd **speed up** every plan rather than freeze.
She sees her poorer clients going to **free AI**, which takes her market.

steps.text: Rush the mediation accreditation and offer Saturday sessions
Use every AI tool to take on more clients cheaply
Cut every household cost except rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to rebuild family law around people, not paperwork. Mediators, counsellors, lawyers who sit with families. I'd be sounding a hopeful note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is just about enough for me. By 2031 I want to be a mediator with my own small client list, not a junior lawyer drafting forms. The risk is money: building that takes savings, and I've got none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd qualify as a mediator and start taking a few paid sessions a month. I'd keep my firm job until the mediation brought in half my pay, maybe 2029. And I'd set up a simple website with booking and use AI to handle the admin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited too. Like I could actually build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner do in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part I can't solve for him. I'd push him to retrain, maybe as a signwriter, something with his hands, since robots come later. He'd probably build the website for my mediation in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be self-employed with no savings. What happens in a bad month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's why I'd keep the firm job till 2029. I've seen what feast or famine does to my partner. I'm not jumping until there's a net.

say: I'd say five years can **rebuild family law** around people.
I'd sound a **hopeful note** about mediators and counsellors.
think: By 2031 I want my own **mediation clients**, not form drafting.
Building that takes **savings**, and I have none.
do: Qualify as a **mediator** and take a few paid sessions monthly.
Keep the **firm job** until mediation pays half.
Set up a **booking website** with AI doing the admin.
feel: **Anxious** but **excited**, like I could build something.
S3.quote: By 2031 I want to be a mediator with my own small client list, not a junior lawyer drafting forms.
fieldNote: Five years turns her fear into a **staged business plan**.
She refuses to **jump without a net**, learning from her partner's swings.
Her partner's future is the **unsolved** part.

steps.text: Qualify as a mediator and take a few paid sessions monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to get this right. Train people, keep humans in decisions about kids, and use AI to make family law cheaper for everyone. I'd be one of the optimists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years suits me. I'd be 37, with years of mediation and AI experience, and I could choose where to land. My worry is the in-between years, because my money is thin the whole way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the mediation course in the next two years without rushing. I'd keep using AI every day at the firm and ask for a pay rise based on the hours it saves. And I'd try to get three months saved before I make any bigger move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy only now and then. Mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything about having children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might. My partner and I said maybe at thirty-two. With a decade's warning I'd want to know I'd landed somewhere before we had a baby. I wouldn't want to be retraining with a newborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask for a raise based on the hours AI saves. Would the partners agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not at first. They'd say the saved hours belong to the firm. But if I can show I'm bringing in more clients, not just working faster, I'd have a case.

I'd want **humans** kept in decisions about children.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's both of us at once, my paperwork and my partner's design work. What would help is cheap, fast routes into new work, like funded mediation courses, and some income while people retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. Everyone asks about one person's job. In our house, two incomes could go in the same year, and nobody plans for that.

headlineQuote: In our house, two incomes could go in the same year, and nobody plans for that.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old** family lawyer at a market-town firm, paid less than at bigger firms.
She uses AI **every day** for financial paperwork and plans to become a **mediator**.
Her partner is a **freelance designer**, so she fears losing two incomes at once.
She grows **alarmed** at AGI by 2028 but sees a path to her own mediation work with more time.
With **no savings**, she won't go self-employed until there's a safety net.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her paperwork and her partner's **design** work could go together.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, fast routes into new work, like **funded mediation** courses.
